title: Dolcetto
description: Piedmont's everyday red: dark, fruity and soft, with a bitter almond finish.
L: The little sweet one, made dry

Dolcetto is a Piedmont grape giving deep purple wines with black cherry, plum, liquorice and a typical bitter almond finish. Acidity is low for Piedmont, tannins moderate. It's made to drink young, a daily wine for the Piedmontese while Barolo ages.

Dolcetto means little sweet one, but the wine is dry. The name probably refers to the grapes' sweetness when eaten, or to their low acidity compared with Barbera and Nebbiolo. Dolcetto ripens early, up to four weeks before Nebbiolo, so it grows on cooler, higher sites that Nebbiolo couldn't ripen.
Not true. The name means little sweet one, but the wines are dry. The name refers to the grape, not the wine.

Look for deep purple colour, dark fruit and a soft, round palate with low acidity and moderate tannin, ending in a slightly bitter, almond note. Compared with Barbera, it has less acidity and more tannin; compared with Nebbiolo, much less tannin and darker colour.
Barbera is high in acidity and low in tannin; Dolcetto the reverse.
Dolcetto gives dark, soft wines with a bitter almond finish
Its name means little sweet one, but the wine is dry
It ripens early, on cooler sites than Nebbiolo
Explain its place in Piedmont's vineyards

Dolcetto grows almost only in Piedmont and nearby Liguria, where it's called Ormeasco. Main zones are Alba, Dogliani, Ovada and Diano d'Alba. Because it ripens early, growers plant it on cooler, higher or north-facing slopes, leaving the warmest sites for Nebbiolo.

Three Dolcetto zones are DOCG: Dogliani, Diano d'Alba and Ovada Superiore. Dogliani, south of Barolo, is considered its spiritual home, where Dolcetto is the main grape rather than a sideline. Dogliani wines are fuller and can age a little more.
Dolcetto fills the cooler sites of Piedmont.
In Piedmont, Dolcetto has lost ground to Barbera and Nebbiolo, which fetch higher prices. A good Dolcetto d'Alba or Dogliani is often a bargain.
Why is Dolcetto planted on cooler slopes?
Early ripening means it doesn't need the warmest sites.
Dolcetto grows in Piedmont, mainly Alba, Dogliani and Ovada
It takes cooler slopes, leaving warm ones for Nebbiolo
Dogliani is its spiritual home and a DOCG
Know how long to keep it

Dolcetto suits everyday Piedmontese food: salumi, vitello tonnato, agnolotti pasta, pizza, roast chicken and mild cheeses. Its soft acidity and moderate tannin make it easy with many dishes. Its bitter finish works well with fatty charcuterie.

Serve at 14 to 16 degrees, slightly cooler than big reds. Most Dolcetto is best within two to three years of the vintage, when fruit is fresh. Dogliani Superiore can age five to eight years. It's usually made in steel, without much oak.
Sweet desserts make dry reds taste sour.
In Piedmont, Dolcetto is often the wine on the table at lunch, while Barolo and Barbaresco wait for special occasions or long ageing. It's honest and fruity rather than complex, and that's its charm.
Most Dolcetto is best drunk within two to three years.
Yes. Its charm is fresh, dark fruit.
Dolcetto suits salumi, pasta and pizza
